title: Drunk Spins: Why the Room Spins and How to Make It Stop
excerpt: Why the room spins when you lie down drunk, what actually stops the spins, why you can feel dizzy the day after drinking, and the warning signs that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Why the room spins when you're drunk, how to stop the spins, why you feel dizzy the day after drinking, and the warning signs that need medical help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the drunk spins are mostly an inner-ear problem. Alcohol seeps into the tiny balance sensors in your ear at a different speed than it seeps into the fluid around them, and for a few hours those sensors send your brain a false signal that you are turning. Lie down, close your eyes, and the room starts to rotate. The same effect can come back in reverse the next morning as it washes out, which is a big part of why you can feel dizzy the day after drinking. Spins are unpleasant but usually harmless on their own. The real dangers are vomiting while lying on your back and mistaking alcohol poisoning for "just the spins." This guide explains what is happening, what actually helps, why next-day dizziness happens, and the signs that mean you need medical help.

**The quick rules:** Stop drinking as soon as the spins start. Sit up, or lie on your side with one foot on the floor, and keep your eyes open on a fixed point. Sip water rather than gulping it. Never leave someone who is very drunk and vomiting alone on their back. The next morning, get up slowly, drink fluids, eat something, and expect the dizziness to fade over the day.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research. It is not a substitute for a doctor. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away if** someone who has been drinking is confused and can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute, or long pauses), has a seizure, has blue-tinged or cold, pale skin, or keeps vomiting while drowsy. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not the spins. **Also get urgent care if** dizziness comes with a sudden severe headache, face drooping, slurred speech that doesn't match how much was drunk, weakness or numbness on one side, double vision, or trouble walking that is far worse than expected. Those can signal a stroke and should never be blamed on a hangover.

## What the Drunk Spins Actually Are

"The spins" is the name for a specific feeling: you lie down after drinking, close your eyes, and it feels like the bed or the room is turning, often in one direction. Opening your eyes or sitting up usually makes it ease off. It often comes with nausea, and for many people it is the moment the night turns from fun to miserable.

Doctors have a name for the physical sign behind it: **positional alcohol nystagmus**, or PAN. Nystagmus means involuntary, flickering eye movements. "Positional" means it shows up or gets worse when your head is in certain positions, such as lying flat or tilted to one side. Researchers studying alcohol and balance described this decades ago, and it is one reason police field sobriety tests check for jerky eye movements.

The key idea is that your brain is getting a false message from your balance system. It isn't simply "you're drunk, so everything feels weird." There is a fairly specific mechanical reason, and once you understand it, the tips for stopping the spins make a lot more sense.

## The Inner-Ear Explainer: Why the Room Spins

Deep inside each ear sits the **vestibular system**, your built-in motion sensor. Part of it is three small, fluid-filled loops called the **semicircular canals**. They detect rotation: nodding, shaking your head, spinning in a chair.

Each canal has a little gel-like flap called the **cupula** sitting across it, with sensitive hair cells at its base. When your head turns, the fluid inside the canal (the **endolymph**) lags behind slightly and pushes on the cupula, bending the hair cells. Your brain reads that bend as "we are rotating."

Normally the cupula and the fluid around it have almost exactly the same density. That matters. Because they weigh the same, gravity doesn't push the cupula one way or the other. Only real head movement bends it. So when you lie still, your brain correctly hears "no rotation."

Alcohol breaks that balance in two stages.

### Stage one: while blood alcohol is rising

Alcohol travels in your blood and moves into the tissues of the inner ear. It reaches the cupula faster than it reaches the surrounding fluid. Alcohol is lighter than water, so for a while the cupula becomes slightly **lighter** than the endolymph around it.

Now gravity has something to work on. When you lie down or tilt your head, the lighter cupula tends to float upward, the way a cork would. That bends the hair cells even though your head isn't actually turning. Your brain gets a steady "you're spinning" signal while your eyes and body say you're lying still. That mismatch is the spins. Researchers usually call this phase **PAN I**, and it tends to show up in the first few hours of drinking, while your blood alcohol level is climbing or near its peak.

### Stage two: as alcohol clears

Later, the process flips. Alcohol leaves the cupula before it leaves the surrounding fluid. For a while the fluid is the lighter one, so the cupula is relatively **heavier** and tends to sink in certain head positions. The false rotation signal returns, often in the opposite direction. This is called **PAN II**, and it can appear several hours after drinking stops, which often means late at night or the next morning.

Between the two phases there's often a quieter stretch when the densities briefly even out. That is why some people feel fine for a while, then get a second round of dizziness the next day.

### Why closing your eyes makes it worse

Your brain builds its sense of balance from three sources: the inner ear, your eyes, and the pressure and position sensors in your muscles and joints. When two of them agree, the brain can overrule the third.

With your eyes open and fixed on something still, your vision tells your brain "nothing is moving," which partly cancels the false ear signal. Close your eyes in a dark room and you remove that check. Now the inner ear is the loudest voice, and it is saying you're spinning. Lying flat makes it worse because that is the position where gravity tugs hardest on the off-balance cupula.

### The rest of the brain is impaired too

The ear isn't the only player. Alcohol also slows the **cerebellum**, the part of the brain that coordinates movement and helps steady your eyes. That's part of why drunk people sway, stumble and have trouble focusing. An impaired cerebellum is worse at correcting the false signal from the ear, so the two problems stack.

## Why the Spins Make You Feel Sick

The nausea that comes with the spins isn't a coincidence. When the signals from your eyes and inner ear disagree, the brain's response looks a lot like motion sickness. It's the same reason some people feel sick reading in a moving car. One long-standing theory is that the brain treats this kind of mismatch as a possible sign of poisoning and triggers vomiting to get rid of it. With alcohol, that's partly true.

On top of that, alcohol irritates the stomach lining directly and increases stomach acid. So you have two separate drivers of nausea at once: the balance mismatch and the gut irritation. For more on settling your stomach the next day, see our [guide to hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025).

## How to Stop the Spins (What Actually Helps)

There is no switch that turns the spins off, because the cause is alcohol sitting in your inner ear and it leaves on its own schedule. But you can make it much less intense, mostly by giving your brain better information to override the false signal.

1. **Stop drinking.** Every extra drink pushes more alcohol into the inner ear and prolongs the first phase. This is the single most important step.
2. **Sit up for a while.** The spins are usually worst when you're flat. Sitting propped up, in a chair or against pillows, often calms things down. Some people find they can only fall asleep sitting up.
3. **Keep your eyes open and fixed on something still.** Pick a spot on the wall, a door frame or a light switch. Giving your eyes a stable target lets vision overrule your inner ear. A dim light is better than total darkness.
4. **Try the "foot on the floor" trick.** Lying on your side near the edge of the bed with one foot planted on the floor is a popular tip, and the logic holds up. The pressure and position signals from your leg give your brain a third vote that says "we are not moving." It doesn't work for everyone, but it costs nothing to try.
5. **Lie on your side, not your back.** This also matters for safety. If you vomit, you're far less likely to inhale it.
6. **Sip water slowly.** Small sips are less likely to upset your stomach than gulping. Water won't flush the alcohol out of your ear any faster, but it helps with dehydration later.
7. **Breathe slowly and stay calm.** Panic makes nausea worse. Slow breathing through the nose can take the edge off.
8. **Get fresh, cool air.** Some people find it helps with nausea, though it has no effect on the spinning itself.

### What doesn't help

- **More drinking** "to level out." It extends the problem.
- **Coffee.** Caffeine doesn't remove alcohol from your blood or your inner ear, and it can make an upset stomach worse.
- **Forcing yourself to throw up.** It doesn't meaningfully lower blood alcohol once the alcohol has been absorbed, it can damage your throat, and it's risky if you're very drunk.
- **Sleeping pills, antihistamines or anything sedating.** Alcohol is already a sedative. Stacking other sedatives on top of it can dangerously slow breathing. That includes over-the-counter motion-sickness pills, sleep aids like ZzzQuil and Benadryl, and "PM" pain relievers.

## When the Spins Are a Warning Sign

For most people at most parties, the spins are just a sign you drank more, or faster, than your body could keep up with. But they show up at the same point in the night as more serious problems, so it's worth knowing how to tell them apart.

### Spins versus alcohol poisoning

Someone with the spins is drunk but awake. They can talk, answer questions, and they feel better when they sit up. Someone with **alcohol poisoning** has so much alcohol in their system that the parts of the brain controlling breathing, heart rate and temperature start to shut down.

Signs of alcohol poisoning include:

- Confusion or stupor, or not being able to wake them up properly
- Vomiting while semi-conscious
- Seizures
- Slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or long gaps between breaths
- Cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin
- Very low body temperature

If you see these, call 911. Don't wait for every sign to appear. Don't leave the person to "sleep it off," and don't put them in a cold shower. Keep them on their side, stay with them, and if they vomit, make sure their airway stays clear. Blood alcohol can keep rising for a while after the last drink as alcohol is still absorbed from the stomach, so someone who seems "just very drunk" can get worse after they pass out.

### The recovery position

If someone is very drunk and drowsy, roll them onto their side with their top knee bent forward to stop them rolling onto their back, and tilt their head slightly back so their airway stays open. This simple step prevents choking on vomit, which is one of the main ways heavy drinking turns deadly.

## Dizzy the Day After Drinking: Why It Happens

Waking up dizzy, lightheaded or a bit off-balance is one of the most common hangover complaints. It usually has more than one cause, and they often overlap.

### 1. The inner ear is still recalibrating

The second phase of positional nystagmus described above can last into the next morning. As alcohol leaves the cupula before it leaves the surrounding fluid, head movements and lying positions can trigger a brief, real sense of spinning or tilting. This tends to be worst when you roll over in bed, sit up suddenly or look up. It typically fades as the alcohol finishes clearing, which takes a number of hours after a heavy night.

### 2. Dehydration and low blood pressure

Alcohol suppresses **vasopressin**, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. That's why you pee so much when you drink. By morning you may be short on fluid, which lowers your blood volume. When you stand up quickly, your blood pressure can briefly drop before your body adjusts, and less blood reaches your brain for a moment. That's the head rush, greying vision or "I need to sit back down" feeling. Doctors call it **orthostatic** (on standing) lightheadedness.

Vomiting or diarrhea the night before makes this worse, because you lose fluid and salts like sodium and potassium. Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers when replacing them is worth it.

### 3. Low blood sugar

Your liver is busy processing alcohol, and while it does, it's worse at releasing stored sugar into your blood. If you drank without eating much, your blood sugar may run low the next morning. That can cause shakiness, sweating, weakness and lightheadedness. Eating something with carbohydrates usually helps within half an hour or so.

### 4. Bad sleep

Alcohol can help you fall asleep, but it fragments sleep in the second half of the night and suppresses REM sleep. Waking up underslept on its own can make you feel foggy and unsteady. We go into the details in our [analysis of alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025).

### 5. Lingering alcohol

After a big night, you may still have alcohol in your blood when you wake up. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour on average, and that varies a lot from person to person. If you stopped drinking at 2 a.m. after eight or ten drinks, part of your morning dizziness may simply be that you are still somewhat drunk. Don't drive until you're confident it has cleared.

### 6. Migraine and other triggers

For some people, alcohol (red wine especially) is a trigger for migraine, and a form called **vestibular migraine** causes episodes of vertigo, sometimes with little or no headache. If you regularly get spinning attacks after drinking, especially with light sensitivity or a history of migraines, it's worth raising with a doctor.

## How to Feel Less Dizzy the Next Morning

- **Get up in stages.** Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before you stand. Hold onto something the first time you get up.
- **Drink fluids early.** Water is fine. If you vomited or had diarrhea, an oral rehydration drink or something with electrolytes can help you recover faster.
- **Eat something simple.** Toast, crackers, a banana, eggs or oatmeal help bring blood sugar back up and are easy on the stomach.
- **Move your head gently.** Quick turns and looking straight up can trigger the leftover inner-ear spin.
- **Rest if you can.** Sleep and time are the main cures for the inner-ear part.
- **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Another drink can mask symptoms for a while by delaying the second phase, but it just postpones the problem and adds more alcohol for your body to clear.
- **Don't drive** while you still feel dizzy or think you might have alcohol in your system.

Most next-day dizziness fades by the afternoon or evening. If it's still strong more than a day after drinking, it probably isn't a hangover, and you should get it checked.

> **When to see a doctor about dizziness after drinking:**
>
> - **Call 911 now** for dizziness with a sudden severe headache, chest pain, fainting, a seizure, one-sided weakness or numbness, face drooping, double vision, or trouble speaking or walking that is out of proportion to how much you drank. These can be signs of a stroke, a heart rhythm problem or a head injury.
> - **Get checked the same day** if you hit your head while drinking (people often don't remember falls), you can't keep fluids down for more than a day, you have black or bloody vomit, or you feel faint every time you stand.
> - **See a doctor soon** if dizziness lasts more than 24 to 48 hours after your last drink, keeps coming back, comes with hearing loss, ringing in one ear or a feeling of fullness in the ear, or if you get spinning attacks even when you haven't been drinking.
> - **Shaking, sweating, a racing heart, anxiety or confusion that starts six hours or more after you stop drinking** can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover, particularly if you've been drinking heavily for days in a row. Withdrawal can become dangerous. Talk to a doctor rather than waiting it out.

## Who Gets the Spins More Easily

There's no good research ranking exactly who gets the spins, but the mechanism makes some patterns predictable:

- **People who drink fast.** The spins are tied to how quickly alcohol builds up in the blood and inner ear. Shots and drinking games push blood alcohol up faster than slowly sipped drinks.
- **People who drink on an empty stomach.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed, so the peak is lower and later.
- **People with a lower body weight**, and often women at the same number of drinks, because the same amount of alcohol produces a higher blood alcohol level.
- **People who don't drink often.** Occasional drinkers tend to feel the effects of alcohol more strongly than regular drinkers at the same blood level.
- **People with existing inner-ear or balance conditions**, such as a history of vertigo or vestibular migraine.

Rising tolerance is not good news, by the way. If you used to get the spins and now never do at the same amount, that's a sign your body has adapted to regular heavy drinking, not that you've become "better" at drinking.

## How to Avoid the Spins Next Time

Since the spins come from how much alcohol reaches your inner ear and how fast, prevention is mostly about pace and amount:

- **Eat a real meal before you start drinking**, ideally with some protein and fat.
- **Pace yourself.** Roughly one standard drink an hour gives your liver a chance to keep up.
- **Alternate with water** or a non-alcoholic drink.
- **Skip shots and drinking games**, which spike your blood alcohol quickly.
- **Stop when you notice early warning signs**, like the room feeling a bit tilted when you turn your head or blurry vision when you look sideways. That's the first phase starting.
- **Count your drinks.** Cocktails and generous home pours often contain two or more standard drinks.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through these habits and the evidence behind each.

## Where Supplements Fit (Honestly)

No supplement stops alcohol from reaching your inner ear, and nothing on a shelf will switch off the spins once they start. If you're very drunk, the right response is to stop drinking and keep yourself safe, not to take something.

Some people use supplements alongside sensible drinking habits to help with how they feel the next day. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, is the one this site focuses on. Lab and animal research suggests it may affect how the body handles alcohol and how alcohol acts on the brain, and there is a small amount of human data. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents the drunk spins or next-day dizziness specifically, and it is not a way to drink more safely. If you want to try DHM as part of a broader plan, two widely used options are [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- The drunk spins come from alcohol changing the density of the balance sensors in your inner ear, which sends your brain a false "you're spinning" signal.
- They're worst lying flat with your eyes closed. Sitting up, keeping your eyes on a fixed point and putting a foot on the floor give your brain better information and usually ease them.
- The effect can reverse and return the next morning as alcohol clears, adding to dehydration, low blood sugar and poor sleep to make you dizzy the day after.
- Stop drinking when the spins start, lie on your side, and never leave a very drunk person alone on their back.
- Confusion, slow breathing, seizures or not waking up mean alcohol poisoning. Call 911. Dizziness with stroke-like symptoms, a head injury, or dizziness that lasts more than a day or two needs a doctor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What causes the drunk spins?**

Mainly your inner ear. Alcohol moves into the small gel-like sensors in your balance canals (the cupula) faster than into the fluid around them, making them lighter for a while. Gravity then bends them when you lie down, and your brain reads that as spinning. This is called positional alcohol nystagmus. Alcohol's effect on the cerebellum, the part of the brain that coordinates balance, makes it harder for your brain to correct the false signal.

**How do you stop the spins when you're drunk?**

Stop drinking, sit up or lie on your side rather than your back, and keep your eyes open on a fixed point in a dimly lit room. Many people find that placing one foot flat on the floor helps, because it gives the brain another signal that you're not moving. Sip water slowly. Nothing removes the alcohol from your inner ear faster, so the spins fade as your body processes it.

**How long do the drunk spins last?**

There's no fixed time. The first wave usually lasts while your blood alcohol is high, often an hour or a few hours, and eases as levels fall. A second, often milder wave can show up several hours later as alcohol clears, which is why some people feel dizzy again the next morning. If dizziness lasts more than a day or two after drinking, see a doctor.

**Why am I dizzy the day after drinking?**

Usually a combination of things: the inner ear's balance sensors are still readjusting as alcohol leaves them, you're dehydrated so your blood pressure dips when you stand, your blood sugar may be low, and alcohol disrupted your sleep. You may also still have some alcohol in your system. Getting up slowly, drinking fluids and eating something usually help it fade by later in the day.

**Is hangover dizziness dangerous?**

Usually not. Mild dizziness or lightheadedness that improves with fluids, food and rest is a normal part of a hangover. Get urgent help if dizziness comes with a sudden severe headache, fainting, chest pain, one-sided weakness or numbness, face drooping, double vision or trouble speaking, or if you hit your head while drinking. Dizziness that lasts more than a day or two, or keeps coming back, should be checked by a doctor.

**Why do the spins get worse when I close my eyes?**

Your brain combines signals from your eyes, inner ears and body to work out whether you're moving. With your eyes open and focused on something still, vision can overrule the false spinning signal from your inner ear. Close your eyes and that check disappears, so the inner ear's message dominates. Lying flat also makes it worse, because that position lets gravity pull hardest on the affected sensors.

**Does the foot-on-the-floor trick actually work?**

It works for some people. Pressure and position signals from your leg and foot give your brain extra evidence that you're not moving, which can help it overrule the inner ear. There's little formal research on the trick itself, but it fits how the balance system works and it's harmless to try. Lying on your side while you do it is also safer if you vomit.

**When are the spins a sign of alcohol poisoning?**

The spins alone are not a sign of alcohol poisoning. A person with the spins is awake, can talk and usually feels better sitting up. Alcohol poisoning looks different: confusion, being hard or impossible to wake, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, or cold, pale or bluish skin. If you see any of these, call 911, keep the person on their side and stay with them.

**Can DHM stop the drunk spins?**

There's no good evidence that DHM or any other supplement stops the spins. The spins come from alcohol in your inner ear, and the only reliable fixes are drinking less, drinking more slowly and stopping once they start. Some people use DHM as part of their routine for next-day comfort, but it isn't a substitute for pacing yourself or a way to make heavy drinking safe.
